# How Vasubandhu found its canonical form

The ASCII form *vasubandhu* is not missing anything that this ​name requires. **Vasubandhu** is the canonical spelling supported by the Devanagari evidence and the tradition's scholarly conventions. This post explains what that form preserves, how it is pronounced, which narratives surround it, ‌and why consistency matters. There are no recovered accents to celebrate; there is something more useful — a spelling whose history can actually be checked.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Vasubandhu
- **ASCII ‌form:** vasubandhu
- **Meaning:** "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school"
- **Domain of influence:** Abhidharma, Yogacara

## Overview

​**Vasubandhu** (*vasubandhu*) — Abhidharma, Yogacara · The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the ​domain "Abhidharma, Yogacara". The name means "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school".

Vasubandhu is the **great systematizer of Buddhist philosophy**: author of the Abhidharmakośa, ​the encyclopedia of Abhidharma that every later school had to answer, and, with his half-brother Asaṅga, co-founder of the Yogācāra, the 'Mind-Only' school that reshaped Mahāyāna thought from India to Japan.

## Mythology

The stories of Vasubandhu place abhidharma, yogacara at the center of a living mythological ​world.

### Origins (Myth)

Vasubandhu appears in buddhist tradition as abhidharma, yogacara. The name's meaning, "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school", shapes the narratives told ​about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Vasubandhu in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Vasubandhu survive ​in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the ‌attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Vasubandhu gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Three Years in Seclusion (The Kośa)

The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu ​withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the ‌Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: ​the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in ‌fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his ​conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism.

### The Begging Letter of Asaṅga ‌(Conversion)

Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a ​note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the ‌Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. ​He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became ​one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be seen whole.

### The Victory over Vasurāta (The Debate)

The biographies carry Vasubandhu to the courts of ‌northern India, where the grammarian-philosopher Vasurāta, champion of an opposing school, had humiliated all comers. Vasubandhu entered the contest — the tradition describes a great assembly of rival teachers and lay patrons gathered ‌to watch — and his opponent was worsted. After the debate he was offered a great patron's gold — and the legends insist that, as a monk, he spent the wealth on ‌works of benefit to the saṅgha and on gifts to the poor. The story matters less as history than as the template it sets: the philosopher's victory is measured not in refutation ​but in what the victor refuses to keep. Every medieval debate culture of the Buddhist world — Nālandā's, Tibet's, Japan's — repeated this scene with Vasubandhu's name in it, and his reputation ​as the undefeated champion of two successive orthodoxies made the later conversion legend necessary: only love, the tradition decided, could have beaten him.

## A Meditation

Vasubandhu is the scholar as religious figure — ​proof that in the Buddhist world, thinking carefully was itself a sacred practice. His two careers look like a contradiction: the great classifier of the mind's parts, then the teacher who said ‌the parts and the world they compose are 'mind-only'. Read together, they form one argument: you must take the world apart completely before you can see what holds it together. His legend ‌conversion turns not on a vision but on a letter from a dying brother — intellect bending at last to love. Modern philosophy of mind still returns to his Viṁśikā, where a ‌dream, a reflection, and the waking world are made to trade places in a few pages. Few ancient authors remain so contemporary: the question of what the world is made of, and ‌whether mind is on the list, is still his question.
